evidence.note: Screenplay written by Oscar Micheaux in 1925, credited to an original story or unpublished Micheaux-authored novel of the same era â€” both the film and its source material share the same 1925 origin and the same term-expiry status. Some film historians (notably Charles Musser) argue the script drew on earlier theatrical works featuring Robeson, including Eugene O'Neill's The Emperor Jones (first published 1921). That play is itself a pre-1930 US publication and also PD by term as of 2026, so even on the broadest reading of the source material no underlying protected work survives.

editorial:
Body and Soul is a 1925 silent race film produced, written, directed, and distributed by Oscar Micheaux through the Micheaux Film Corporation. It is Paul Robeson's only film with an African American director and his motion picture debut; he plays dual roles as an escaped convict posing as a preacher who extorts and brutalizes a Black Southern community, and as the virtuous twin brother that community deserves. Micheaux originally delivered nine reels, but New York's Motion Picture Commission rejected the cut twice â€” citing incitement to crime, immorality, and sacrilege â€” forcing it down to five reels before it could open. The director's nine-reel version is a lost film; what survives is the censorship-mandated compromise, itself selected for the Library of Congress National Film Registry in 2019.

For a creator sourcing footage, the 1925 print is firmly public domain in the US â€” the 95-year maximum term expired January 1, 2021, and the AFI confirms the film is freely accessible. The real trap is provenance: the two commercially available versions (Criterion's 2007 Paul Robeson DVD, built from the George Eastman Museum restoration, and Kino Lorber's 2016 'Pioneers of African-American Cinema' Blu-ray with DJ Spooky's new score) each carry their own copyright in the restoration work, and the Kino release adds a fully protected contemporary musical composition. Ripping from a commercial disc or licensed stream does not give you the free version â€” it gives you someone else's protected expression wrapped around the free original. Use a copy verifiably sourced from the unrestored public-domain print.
faq: Can I use footage from the Kino Lorber or Criterion release freely?

No. Both commercial releases carry independent restoration copyright â€” Criterion through the George Eastman Museum's restoration work, Kino Lorber through its own restoration decisions plus DJ Spooky's separately protected 2016 score. The underlying 1925 print is public domain, but those specific versions are not. Source footage from a copy traceable to the unrestored print, such as the uploads available on the Internet Archive.
Does Paul Robeson's performance in this film create any rights issues?

Robeson's 1925 on-screen performance is public domain along with the film â€” US copyright law does not recognize a separate performance right that outlasts the film's own term. Straightforward documentary or editorial use of footage is generally safe. Some US states recognize a post-mortem right of publicity (Robeson died in 1976), which can restrict commercial exploitation â€” advertising, merchandise, or endorsement contexts â€” that trades on his name or likeness. Non-commercial and transformative uses are typically outside that right's reach.
